claims.text: Metal ranks next only to clay among Indian crafts and is used as brass, copper and bell metal for articles from kitchenware to fine gold and enamel jewellery.

quotes.quote: Metal figures only next to clay in the composition of the Indian crafts and has been universally used in the form of brass, copper, bell metal etc. covering a very wide range of articles from kitchenware to fine gold and enamel jewellery.

claims.text: The range of Indian metalware is so vast and varied that enumerating it comprehensively would be almost impossible; moreover each region has its own special designs and processes, and each metal again shows wide variety.

quotes.quote: So vast and varied is the range covered by metalware in India that it would be almost an impossible task to enumerate them in any comprehensive manner.
Moreover each region has its own special designs and processes. In each metal again there is a wide variety.

claims.text: Indian Metalware (1961) describes gold and silver utensil making as restricted to a few centres, while brass and copper ware forms an extensive industry all over the country.

quotes.locator: Indian Metalware, chapter 'brass and copper ware', pp. 32-44, p. 32
quotes.quote: The manufacture of household utensils in gold and silver is restricted to a few centres since the demand is comparatively limited but that in brass and copper forms an extensive industry all over the country.

claims.text: Dhokra is the lost-wax casting of brass, bronze and bell-metal objects, a living tradition across Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Telangana, Odisha and Madhya Pradesh.

quotes.quote: The process of casting brass, bronze and bell-metal objects using the lost-wax technique, Dhokra is a living tradition practised by various artisan communities across the present-day states of Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Telangana, Odisha and Madhya Pradesh.

claims.text: Bidriware is a damascening technique of silver and sometimes gold or, rarely, copper inlay against a darker base alloy, named after the town of Bidar in present-day Karnataka.

quotes.quote: A technique of damascening, bidriware features metallic inlay against a darker base metal alloy layer.
The technique derives its name from the town of Bidar, in present-day Karnataka, India, once a capital of the Bahmani Sultanate

claims.text: Koftgari is a damascening technique originating in Persia in which gold or silver is inlaid or encrusted on blued metal, usually steel or iron.

is a decorative metalwork technique in which gold or silver is inlaid or encrusted on blued metal, usually steel or iron

claims.text: Thewa, practised since the mid-eighteenth century by a small number of families in Rajasthan, fuses openwork gold leaf onto coloured glass.

quotes.quote: An intricate and distinctive goldsmithing craft practised since the mid-eighteenth century by a small number of families in Rajasthan in northwest India, thewa (Rajasthani, 'setting') involves fusing openwork gold leaf onto coloured glass.

claims.text: Tarkashi inlays thin metal wire on shisham and other hardwood and is practised mainly in Uttar Pradesh and, more recently, Rajasthan.

quotes.quote: A decorative craft in which thin metal wire is inlaid on shisham and other hardwood, tarkashi (Urdu and Persian: taar, 'wire'; kashi, 'drawing') is practised primarily in Uttar Pradesh, and more recently Rajasthan, in northern India.

claims.text: Making utilitarian and devotional articles of brass and bronze is a speciality of the Kansari community of Odisha, practised since the eleventh century.

quotes.quote: Practised since the eleventh century, the craft of making utilitarian and devotional articles from brass and bronze is a speciality of the Kansari community of Odisha, in India.

claims.text: The craft of the Thatheras of Jandiala Guru is the traditional technique of making brass and copper utensils in Punjab.

quotes.quote: The craft of the Thatheras of Jandiala Guru constitutes the traditional technique of manufacturing brass and copper utensils in Punjab.

claims.text: Handheld metal mirrors called val kannadi are still made in Aranmula, Kerala, a craft guarded by hereditary families where metal mirror-making seems to have died out elsewhere.

quotes.quote: Whereas metal mirror-making practices seem to have died out elsewhere in the world, a remarkable crafts survival, which was zealously guarded by hereditary families, is still prevalent in Kerala in southern India.
The verdant village of Aranmula is home to an exotic traditional craft of making handcrafted, handheld metal mirrors known as val kannadi.

claims.text: A distinct style of bronze sculpture developed under the Chola empire in present-day Tamil Nadu from the tenth to the thirteenth century CE, made chiefly by lost-wax casting.

quotes.quote: From the tenth to the thirteenth century CE a distinct style of bronze sculpture developed under the Chola empire in present-day Tamil Nadu in southern India.
Made chiefly using the lost-wax method of casting, these sculptures are widely acknowledged for the excellence of their craftsmanship and figural elegance.

is enclosed in a mixture of clay and cowdung.

lede.text: Metal ranks next only to clay among Indian crafts, used as brass, copper and bell metal for articles from kitchenware to fine gold and enamel jewellery, and each region has its own special designs and processes.

Indian Metalware (1961) describes gold and silver utensil making as restricted to a few centres while brass and copper ware forms an extensive industry all over the country, brass being an alloy of copper and zinc and bronze one of copper and tin.

Its makers include the Kansari community of Odisha and the Thatheras of Punjab, who hammer brass, bell metal and copper vessels, and the dhokra casters of Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Telangana, Odisha and Madhya Pradesh, who cast brass, bronze and bell metal by lost wax.

The earliest firm evidence for metallic zinc production is from India, which also made wootz, an ultra-high carbon steel, while bidriware sets silver and sometimes gold inlay in a darker, mainly zinc alloy and koftgari inlays gold or silver on blued steel or iron.

sentences.text: Indian Metalware (1961) records that utensils are hammered from sheet or country brass, cast in moulds, or partly cast and partly beaten, that copper vessels are never cast, and that buyers prefer hammered ware, which only superior brass and bronze allow.
Surfaces are ornamented by repousse, by damascening, which encrusts one metal on another as wire, by flat encrusting as in bidri, and by enamelling, which fuses mineral substances over the metal.

Dhokra is the lost-wax casting of brass, bronze and bell-metal objects in Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Telangana, Odisha and Madhya Pradesh, and takes its name from the Dhokra Damar metal artisans of West Bengal.

The Kansari community of Odisha makes utilitarian and devotional articles of brass and bronze, a craft believed to have originated around the eleventh century, and the Thatheras of Jandiala Guru make brass and copper utensils in Punjab.
Bidriware sets metal inlay against a darker base alloy and is named after the town of Bidar, while koftgari inlays or encrusts gold or silver on blued steel or iron.

A National Institute of Design student study describes Bastar's wrought iron craft, practised mainly by the Lohar community, as iron heated and beaten to shape, and Bastar Iron Craft and Wrought Iron Crafts of Dindori are registered GIs.

Thewa fuses openwork gold leaf onto coloured glass in Rajasthan, tarkashi inlays thin metal wire on shisham and other hardwood in Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan, and Aranmula in Kerala still makes handheld metal mirrors called val kannadi, a craft guarded by hereditary families.

Sources differ on bronze: Indian Metalware holds that most surviving ancient metal figures seem to be of copper or brass, while Srinivasan and Ranganathan count the Chola icons among the finest bronze castings in the world.
Indian brass is copper and zinc, usually two parts copper to one or one and a half parts zinc, and a very small quantity of lead is often added to make it soft and malleable.
Bronze is given as 7 parts of copper and 2 parts of tin, pure bronze being used for hammered plates while cast articles are chiefly of an impure alloy called Bharan or Toul.
Bell metal, called kasa, kansa or kansya, is a type of bronze, but sources differ on its make-up, from 7 parts of copper to 2 parts of tin to lead and brass mixed.

Indian Metalware (1961) says brass for the images of Banaras is mixed with gold, silver, iron, tin, lead and mercury into a mixture of 8 metals deemed a perfect alloy, and panchaloha, five metals, is a sacred alloy traditionally used for temple idols.
The bidri body is an alloy of mainly zinc with small quantities of copper, tin and other metals, and its composition differs from region to region.

Aranmula mirrors are a binary copper-tin alloy of 32-33 per cent tin that optimises the delta phase of bronze, and the earliest and continuing use of rapidly quenched high-tin bronzes is from the Indian subcontinent.
Wootz, the anglicised form of ukku, a word for steel, was an ultra-high carbon steel with 1-2% carbon believed to have been used for Damascus blades.
Moradabad is known as peetalnagri or brass city, but a 2023 field study found aluminium the main substitute metal, making up around 50-60 percent of its metal products.
In lost-wax casting a wax model is coated in clay, molten metal takes the place of the escaping wax, and the figure is then chased with hand tools.

A dhokra caster moulds a core of clay, rice husk and water, covers it with threads of beeswax mixed with resin, coats the wax model with clay, and often dewaxes and casts at the same time in a pit furnace.

In a Pondicherry workshop making Chola-style bronzes, the dried mould is heated so that the wax melts out and is baked further, and since every mould is broken and used only once, each image made there is unique.
Sheet copper or brass is marked out with compasses, cut with scissors called Katari, shaped by alternate heating and hammering, and turned on the lathe.
Thatheras hammer flattened plates into curved vessels over tiny wood-fired stoves, and Kansari teams hammer reheated ingots on stone, layering new ingots so that several bowls or plates form at once.

Filigree silver is drawn into flat wire, twisted like minute rope, packed into leaves and flowers, and soldered with soldering salt on mica in the furnace, and Indian Metalware (1961) records that much of this work is done by children of about 8 to 10 years.
For koftgari the object is blued by heat alone, and in teh-i-nishan grooves are cut two-thirds as deep as the wire's diameter for a durable inlay flush with the surface.
Aranmula makers overcome the brittleness of delta bronze by casting a blank no more than a couple of millimetres thick in a closed crucible-cum-mould.

Zinc is among the hardest ancient metals to smelt because it volatilises at about the temperature needed to smelt its ore, and at Zawar its vapour was drawn down through retorts with condensers and cooled to solid zinc metal.
Bidri is patinated in a boiling slurry of ammonium chloride and Bidar fort clay, which gives a jet-black protective layer of zinc oxide and hydroxide while the inlay keeps its lustre.
Rolla and colleagues report that the black patina is accredited to copper in the alloy, since none of the zinc compounds is black, and found 91.681% zinc and 6.110% copper on a patinated surface.
The flux for enamel is always borax, sometimes with tin oxide for opacity, and colours come from metallic salts such as cobalt oxide for blue and copper oxide for green.

Indian Metalware says gold takes a far greater range of enamel colours than silver, and silver more than copper and brass, while the brilliant reds of Jaipur, Lucknow and Banaras are the most difficult to produce.
According to Colonel Hendley, quoted in Indian Metalware, Jaipur copper enamels admit only white, black and pink, and even the pink adheres with difficulty.
The Delhi iron pillar's absence of corrosion has been linked to its composition, the high purity of its wrought iron, its phosphorus content and the distribution of slag.

Copper hardens when hammered and can be brought to a sharp edge, and Impart says the Kansari forging process makes brass and bell-metal utensils virtually unbreakable, vulnerable only at joints kept to a minimum.
The silvery-white delta phase gives the Aranmula mirror its high reflectivity, and the alloy is hard enough to take a high polish without distortion.
Wootz is an ultra-high carbon steel showing superplasticity, and European smiths failed to copy Damascus blades, Rao and Biswas point out, because they forged only low carbon steels at white heat.
A finished thewa piece is cooled slowly because rapid cooling would shatter the glass, and a polished silver or tin foil beneath the glass reflects light and intensifies its colour.
The temple bells of India are celebrated for the depth and purity of their tones.
Fairly extensive evidence shows ancient mining of copper ores in the Khetri region of Rajasthan in about the 3rd-2nd millennium BC.
The deepest ancient gold mines in the world are in the Maski region of Karnataka, and the Aravalli region ranks among the few major ancient silver-producing sites.

Indian Metalware places a hornblende schist east of Nirmal as the source of the magnetic iron long used for Damascus steel, and an Expedition article calls the Chota Nagpur hills India's mineral belt, where tribal people smelted copper and, until recently, iron.

Bronze casting flourished at Swamimalai because the Kaveri riverbed was said to have the right clay, alluvial clays from the Pampa supplied Aranmula's moulds, and Bidar fort clay loses its power to blacken bidri after a few uses.
Swamimalai in Thanjavur district is the best-known centre today for the lost-wax bronze casting that originated in the Chola period, a technology rooted across the Tamil region.
Major dhokra centres include Bastar and Kondagaon, Ranchi, Bankura, Birbhum and Bardhaman, Dhenkanal, Koraput and Mayurbhanj, Adilabad, and Betul.
Kansari metalware is largely concentrated in the Odisha districts of Ganjam, Puri, Cuttack and Dhenkanal, and the works of Kantilo in Nayagarh district are well known throughout the state.
Bidar remains a chief centre of bidriware alongside Hyderabad, and Indian Metalware named Jaipur, Alwar, Sialkot, Travancore, Kashmir and Bidar as the chief centres of damascened work.
Cuttack was probably the earliest centre of Indian silver filigree, which spread south to Trichinopoly and Karimnagar and north to Jhansi.

Indian Metalware called Banaras the first city in India for cast mythological images in brass and copper, and Mirzapur one of the most important centres of the brass utensil industry in Uttar Pradesh.
Thewa artisans continue to practise in Pratapgarh district, and Mainpuri remains a major tarkashi centre, its work considered the finest.
According to Indian Metalware, each Indian state has two or three centres noted for their copper and brass ware.
Copper artefacts of about the sixth millennium BC are reported from pre-Indus Baluchistan, and the statue of a dancing girl from Mohenjodaro is among the earliest bronze castings in the world.

Sources differ on dating Mohenjodaro's metal: Indian Metalware says copper objects were known there in about 1,500 B.C., while Srinivasan and Ranganathan date its gold and silver ornaments to about 3000 BC.

Lost-wax casting is known in India from at least the 3rd millennium, and from the ninth century it became the signature of Chola image-making, a distinct bronze style that developed from the tenth to the thirteenth century.

Iron seems to have been used in India from about the late second millennium BC, and the Delhi iron pillar, over 7 m high, is dated by one source to about 400 A.D. and by another to the Gupta period of the 3rd c. AD.

The earliest firm evidence for metallic zinc production is from India, the Zawar area of Rajasthan holds unique evidence of its extensive, semi-industrial production, and the Rasaratnakara describes its downward distillation.

The Indian crucible steel process is likely to have started in Tamil Nadu before the Christian era, Zaky pointed out that Arabs took wootz ingots to Damascus, and by the late 1600s tens of thousands of ingots were traded from the Coromandel coast to Persia.
Sources differ on when bidri began, from about the 14th century to the fifteenth century, and the earliest evidence of a bidriware object is a Deccani painting dated to about 1625.

Koftgari likely spread to South Asia in the fourteenth century with the Timurid invasion of the Punjab, was used mainly on weapons and armour between the sixteenth and nineteenth centuries, and turned to everyday objects as arms manufacture declined.

According to Katyal (2016), cited by an ISID study, approximately 40-50 percent of India's metal craft exports originate in Moradabad, and in 2022-23 the district's metal craft and related exports were Rs 61.96 billion, 60 percent of its total.

Sources differ on Moradabad's workforce: the National Innovation Council counted 3.5 lakh people in 2014 and a 2020-21 export plan puts employment at 3,50,000, while local voices interviewed in 2023 said artisans had dwindled from five lakh to 2.5 lakh.
An Export Promotion Council for Handicrafts newsletter calls India the largest brass metal ware producer in the world and the second-largest manufacturer of metal works after China.

Sources differ on demand: Impart reports it steadily declining for Kansari wares and an Expedition article says households moved to aluminium and plastic, while Behera finds the brass and bell-metal industry of undivided Puri district, with 1,370 skilled artisans in 1961, not declined despite stiff competition.

Registered metal-craft GIs include Swamimalai Bronze Icons, Bell Metal Ware of Datia and Tikamgarh, Silver Filigree of Karimnagar, Bikaner Usta Kala Craft, Bastar Iron Craft and Uttarakhand Tamta Product.
Other metal GIs include Thanjavur Art Plate, Dindigul Locks, Moradabad Metal Craft, Aligarh Tala, Mainpuri Tarkashi, Jharkhand Dokra Craft and Ladakh Chilling Metal Work.

The registry lists Bidriware within April 2005 to March 2006 while Impart gives 2008; it lists Bastar Dhokra (application 83) within April 2008 to March 2009 and Bastar Dhokra (Logo) (application 387) within April 2013 to March 2014, and Impart, citing application 387, gives 2014.
Bidri artisans face high costs of silver and saltpetre clay and poor pay, and teh-i-nishan koftgari has become rare partly because deeper grooves need more precious metal.
Ganga-Jamuna names work in which two colours meet side by side, after the two rivers, as when gold and silver wire share one pattern.
Bidri inlay ranges from tarkashi wire and tehnishan sheet inlay to low-relief zarnishan and the high-relief zarbuland of Lucknow, and the poppy is among its oldest patterns.
Moradabad engraving is sada, cut through tinning so that the brass shines gold, or sia kalam, with the floral design in low relief against coloured lac.

Indian Metalware (1961) says Swami work, raised Puranic gods and animal figures on medallions and niches, had until recently been the characteristic feature of Madras gold and silver plate, the best made in Tanjore, while Kerala joins small silver chakrams into lattice work.
Dhokra surfaces carry threaded false filigree cast in one with the piece, and tarkashi is marked by a profusion of small dots called bhiriyan.

Vessel shapes come from fruit shells such as the gourd, lotus and lily leaves and animal horns, and Indian Metalware (1961) observed that Muslims preferred ornamental repoussed articles while Hindus, except for objects of religious significance, generally preferred severely plain utensils.
Koftgari weapons often bore calligraphic religious verses and floral patterns, and Rajput arms featured the sun and moon of the clans' ancestry.
Indian Metalware notes that copper cooking and eating utensils have to be tinned before they can be used with safety.
The copper, brass and alloys of the Thatheras are believed to be beneficial for health, and Ayurveda considers brass and bell metal medicinal and ideal for food utensils.
An account of Pondicherry bronze casting reports that exposure to metal heated up to 1000 degrees Celsius leads to eye problems and hair fall, and long hours on the floor to chronic back pain.
